title: Laravel AI SDK 1.1: build an agent with Agent Skills and human approval
summary: Use SKILL.md skills that load on demand and approvable tools that pause for a person, with the ownership and trust checks the SDK leaves to you.

html:
The short versionSince v1.1.0 (5 October 2026), the Laravel AI SDK can give an agent skills: folders with a SKILL.md file that the model sees as a one-line catalogue entry and loads in full only when a task needs it. Combine skills with approvable tools, and the agent can follow your written procedures while a person still signs off on anything risky, such as a refund. Two things stay your job: deciding which skill text you trust, and checking who is allowed to approve.

Most agent prompts grow the same way. Someone adds the refund rules, then the tone guide, then the edge cases, and soon every request carries thousands of tokens of instructions that are irrelevant to it. Agent Skills fix that by keeping each procedure in its own folder and loading it on demand. This guide builds a small billing support agent in Laravel that uses a refund-policy skill and asks a human before issuing any refund above $50.

Why it matters now

The laravel/ai v1.1.0 release on 5 October 2026 added the HasSkills contract and the LoadSkill tool, and made the SDK's built-in tools (MCP, sub-agent, similarity search and filesystem tools) able to require approval. Approval for your own tools already existed. v1.2.0 followed on 7 October with model-default and structured-output fixes; it does not change skills or approvals, so everything below applies to 1.1 and later. Requirements: PHP 8.3+ and Laravel 12.62+ or 13.15+.

1Install the SDK and create the agent

Install the package, publish its config and migrations, and run the migrations. The migrations create the two conversation tables (agent_conversations and agent_conversation_messages), which approvals depend on later.

Bashcomposer require laravel/ai
php artisan vendor:publish --provider="Laravel\Ai\AiServiceProvider"
php artisan migrate
php artisan make:agent SupportAgent

Put your provider key in .env (for example ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY). The default text provider in config/ai.php is OpenAI; you can change it there or pass provider: when prompting.

2Write the skill as a folder

A skill is a directory under resources/skills with a SKILL.md file. The YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) frontmatter needs a description, which tells the model when to use the skill. The name is optional and defaults to the directory name. Other files in the folder are bundled with the skill and readable on request.

Textresources/skills/
└── refund-policy/
    ├── SKILL.md
    └── references/edge-cases.md
Markdown---
name: refund-policy
description: Use when a customer asks for a refund or disputes a charge.
---

# Refund policy

1. Look up the invoice with the LookupInvoice tool. Never guess amounts.
2. Full refunds are allowed within 30 days of payment.
3. After 30 days, offer account credit instead of a refund.
4. Refund at most the amount paid on that invoice.
5. For chargebacks or partial refunds, read references/edge-cases.md first.

This format follows the open Agent Skills specification, so the same folder can also be used by coding agents. Laravel reads only name, description and the body; it does not enforce the spec's naming rules, so keep names lowercase with hyphens yourself.

3Give the agent its skills

Implement HasSkills and return skill sources from skills(). A source can be a directory path, a Skill object, or a closure that returns Skill objects, which is how you load per-team skills from your database.

PHPnamespace App\Ai\Agents;

use App\Ai\Tools\IssueRefund;
use App\Ai\Tools\LookupInvoice;
use App\Models\User;
use Laravel\Ai\Concerns\RemembersConversations;
use Laravel\Ai\Contracts\Agent;
use Laravel\Ai\Contracts\Conversational;
use Laravel\Ai\Contracts\HasSkills;
use Laravel\Ai\Contracts\HasTools;
use Laravel\Ai\Promptable;
use Laravel\Ai\Skills\Skill;

class SupportAgent implements Agent, Conversational, HasSkills, HasTools
{
    use Promptable, RemembersConversations;

    public function __construct(public User $user) {}

    public function instructions(): string
    {
        return 'You help customers with billing. Follow the matching skill before acting.';
    }

    public function skills(): iterable
    {
        return [
            resource_path('skills'),            // listed first, so it wins name clashes
            fn () => $this->user->team->skills->map(
                fn ($s) => new Skill($s->name, $s->description, $s->instructions)
            ),
        ];
    }

    public function tools(): iterable
    {
        return [new LookupInvoice($this->user), new IssueRefund($this->user)];
    }
}

What happens at run time:

  • The SDK adds one LoadSkill tool. Its description is the catalogue: one - name: description line per skill, sorted by name. That is all the model sees up front.

  • When the model calls LoadSkill with a name, it gets the skill body wrapped in <skill_content> plus a list of bundled files. Calling it again with a path returns one file.

  • Bundled files over 256 KB, binary files and paths outside the skill folder are refused. The tool returns text only; it never runs scripts.

  • When two skills share a name, the source listed first wins. Keep your own directory first so a team's database skill cannot replace refund-policy.

  • If you return directories from skills(), resources/skills is used only if you list it. If skills() returns nothing, no LoadSkill tool is added.

  • Folders are discovered one level deep: skills/billing/refunds/SKILL.md is not found unless you list skills/billing as its own source.

  • The closure runs whenever the catalogue is built, which is on every prompt, not only when a skill is chosen. Keep that query cheap or cache it.

  • Invalid YAML in a frontmatter block throws an exception and fails the prompt. A file with no frontmatter or no description is skipped silently, so check that new skills actually appear in the catalogue.

4Make the risky tool approvable

A tool becomes approvable when it implements Approvable and uses the InteractsWithApprovals trait. Approvable tools need approval by default. Override needsApproval() to decide per call, and return Approval::required() with a reason the reviewer will read.

PHPnamespace App\Ai\Tools;

use App\Models\Invoice;
use App\Models\User;
use Illuminate\Contracts\JsonSchema\JsonSchema;
use Laravel\Ai\Approvals\Approval;
use Laravel\Ai\Concerns\InteractsWithApprovals;
use Laravel\Ai\Contracts\Approvable;
use Laravel\Ai\Contracts\Tool;
use Laravel\Ai\Tools\Request;

class IssueRefund implements Approvable, Tool
{
    use InteractsWithApprovals;

    public function __construct(protected User $user) {}

    public function description(): string
    {
        return 'Refund part or all of a paid invoice, in cents.';
    }

    public function schema(JsonSchema $schema): array
    {
        return [
            'invoice_id' => $schema->string()->required(),
            'amount_cents' => $schema->integer()->required(),
        ];
    }

    protected function needsApproval(Request $request): Approval|bool
    {
        return $request->integer('amount_cents') > 5000
            ? Approval::required('Refunds above $50 need a person to approve them.')
            : false;
    }

    public function handle(Request $request): string
    {
        // Check permissions here too: approval is not authorization.
        $invoice = Invoice::where('team_id', $this->user->team_id)
            ->where('number', (string) $request->string('invoice_id'))
            ->firstOrFail();

        $amount = min($request->integer('amount_cents'), $invoice->paid_cents);

        // The tool call ID is stable. With a unique index on idempotency_key,
        // a retry or a double-clicked approval cannot refund twice.
        $refund = $invoice->refunds()->firstOrCreate(
            ['idempotency_key' => $request->toolCallId()],
            ['amount_cents' => $amount],
        );

        return "Refunded {$refund->amount_cents} cents on invoice {$invoice->number}.";
    }
}

You can also change the rule where the agent registers the tool, with (new IssueRefund($user))->requireApproval('Reason') or ->withoutApproval(). Since v1.1 the same two methods work on the SDK's built-in tools, which do not need approval unless you ask for it. For example, call requireApproval() on an MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool that writes data.

5Pause, show the reviewer, then resume

When the model calls a gated tool, the run stops before executing it. The response tells you so:

PHP$response = SupportAgent::make(user: $user)
    ->forUser($user)
    ->prompt('Please refund invoice INV-1042, I was charged twice.');

if ($response->hasPendingApprovals()) {
    // Each item has id, tool, arguments and reason.
    return [
        'conversation_id' => $response->conversationId,
        'approvals' => $response->pendingApprovals,
    ];
}

Resuming needs the paused turn's history, which is why the agent uses RemembersConversations. Without stored history (or history passed with withMessages()) the SDK throws ApprovalNotResumableException. The reviewer's decision goes back in as a Decisions object keyed by tool call ID:

PHPuse App\Ai\Agents\SupportAgent;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;
use Laravel\Ai\Approvals\Decision;
use Laravel\Ai\Approvals\Decisions;
use Laravel\Ai\Models\Conversation;

Route::post('/support/{conversation}/decide', function (Request $request, Conversation $conversation) {
    $user = $request->user();

    // The SDK does not check ownership when you resume. You must.
    abort_unless(
        $conversation->participant_type === $user->getMorphClass()
            && (string) $conversation->participant_id === (string) $user->getKey(),
        404,
    );

    $decisions = collect($request->validate([
        'decisions' => ['required', 'array'],
        'decisions.*' => ['boolean'],
    ])['decisions'])->map(fn (bool $ok) => $ok
        ? Decision::approve()
        : Decision::reject('A reviewer declined this refund.'));

    $response = SupportAgent::make(user: $user)
        ->continue($conversation->id, as: $user)
        ->prompt(Decisions::from($decisions->all()));

    return ['message' => $response->text];
})->middleware('auth');

In a real app, the person deciding is usually a support lead rather than the customer. Then replace the ownership check with a policy that allows leads of the same team, and keep the 404 for everyone else.

Details worth knowing:

  • Every pending call needs a decision. Unknown, missing or already-resolved IDs throw ApprovalMismatchException, which renders as HTTP 409 with the pending list. Decisions::from([...])->rejectRemaining('...') covers calls you did not list.

  • A rejection with a message is returned to the model so it can reply, for example by offering credit. A rejection without a message stops the run.

  • Decision::edit([...]) lets the reviewer change the arguments before the tool runs. It exists in the v1.1 source but is not yet in the docs.

  • Approval also works with stream(), queue() and the broadcast methods. Streams emit a tool_approval_request event, and the SDK dispatches ToolApprovalRequested and ToolApprovalResolved events you can listen to for notifications and audit logs.

6Test the rules, not the model

The two things you own, the approval rule and the skill content, can be tested without calling a provider:

PHPuse App\Ai\Tools\IssueRefund;
use Laravel\Ai\Tools\LoadSkill;
use Laravel\Ai\Tools\Request;

test('large refunds need approval, small ones do not', function () {
    $tool = new IssueRefund(User::factory()->create());

    expect($tool->shouldRequestApproval(new Request(['amount_cents' => 9900])))->not->toBeNull()
        ->and($tool->shouldRequestApproval(new Request(['amount_cents' => 1200])))->toBeNull();
});

test('the refund skill loads with its bundled files', function () {
    $result = (new LoadSkill([resource_path('skills')]))
        ->handle(new Request(['name' => 'refund-policy']));

    expect($result)->toContain('<skill_content name="refund-policy">')
        ->toContain('references/edge-cases.md');
});

For controller tests, SupportAgent::fake() stops real provider calls, and AgentResponse::fakeWithPendingApprovals([...]) builds a paused response so you can test the reviewer screen.

Common mistakesTrusting database skills: a skill body is effectively extra system instructions, so a team admin who can edit one can steer your agent. Resuming without an ownership check: paused turns are matched by conversation, not by user. Assuming the whole step waits: only the gated call pauses, and other tool calls in the same step run immediately. Retrying the same decisions after a failure: the approved tool has already run and its result is stored, so continue with a normal message instead. Trusting the SDK to stop double submissions: a double-click or a second tab may resume the same turn twice, so make the side effect idempotent as in step 4.

Security: treat skills like code

Skills are a new supply chain. In February 2026, Snyk scanned 3,984 public skills and reported 76 confirmed malicious payloads; 91% of the malicious skills combined malicious code with prompt injection. Anthropic's own guidance is to use only skills you wrote or audited. For a Laravel app that means:

  • Review skill folders in pull requests like code, and do not copy third-party skills in without reading every file.

  • Treat tenant-editable skills as untrusted input. Limit which tools they can influence, and never let the model's choice replace a permission check (OWASP calls this excessive agency).

  • Write approval reasons and argument displays for humans: show "Refund $99.00 on INV-1042 (paid $99.00)", not raw IDs. Reviewers who see vague prompts many times a day start approving everything.

When not to use it

  • A few short instructions: a static system prompt is simpler, easier to test and avoids an extra model round-trip to load the skill.

  • Deterministic rules: if "refund within 30 days" can be computed, compute it in the tool and return the answer. Skills are for judgement and procedure, not arithmetic.

  • Facts that change often: product data and order history belong in a lookup tool or retrieval, not in a skill file.

  • High-volume, low-risk actions: approving each one trains reviewers to click without reading. Use a threshold in needsApproval() so people see only the calls that matter.

Used this way, skills keep the prompt small and the procedures in version control, and approvals put a person in front of the few actions that cost money. The ownership check and the trust boundary around skill text are what make it safe to ship.
